aide.views.def.fragilite: Who is irreplaceable. For each person, the timeslots that would fall below the minimum headcount if they withdrew — and, the decisive column, those nobody else could take over that day. The second view lists the stands held by a single skilled person, which points to where to recruit or train. The versatile “ninja” staff are counted separately, as backup.
aide.views.def.former: Who to train, typology by typology. A typology is listed when the staffing need says it is short, or when the fragility finds a stand held by a single specialist or none; the figures are those of these two tabs, never recomputed. Candidates are the beginners and the autonomous of the typology — never a referent, a polyvalent or somebody without the competence —, ranked by the tension days they are available on, then wish, then level. A typology without a candidate is a matter of recruitment. Without a persisted schedule, only the staffing need speaks. The tab exports as CSV; moving somebody up a level stays a gesture of the Competences grid.
aide.views.def.pauses: The rotation of legal breaks, day by day and stand by stand: who steps out from when to when, one at a time, and who relays. The solver requires a break that is owed to be takeable — a gap, or a colleague on the stand — without saying at which minute it is taken; the screen lays it as late as possible. A second section lists the meal breaks and how many minutes are missing when the grid leaves no room — the days in red are the ones the solver refuses. Below, the catering of the day: how many people are on their meal break, hour by hour and per location, midday and evening — how many sandwiches to prepare, and where to take them. Nobody is named there, minors are counted apart; “The whole event as CSV” exports every day at once.

aide.intro.subtitle: How to use the application: what each screen is for, how to configure the solver, how to read a result and what to fix when a schedule is not feasible. This page reads no data and stays available while a solve is running.

aide.start.title: Getting started
aide.start.summary: The full cycle of an edition: collect, build, solve, publish, follow up.
aide.start.intro: The application puts your staff on seats. A seat is a place to hold on a stand during one timeslot. The solver creates none of them: it chooses who fills the ones your stands and timeslots already describe. Everything is therefore decided when you enter the data.
aide.start.classeur: Three things change compared to a spreadsheet. The legal framework is checked continuously. A late change is replayed without redoing everything. And the schedule you send out is dated: the application knows who received which version.
aide.start.step1: Pick or create the edition. Nothing travels from one edition to another.
aide.start.step3: Open the availability collection with the “notify” box ticked: everyone receives the link to their espace and declares there their absences and wishes. The staff records and the timeslots must therefore already exist.
aide.start.step4: Apply or refuse the declarations you receive, then close the collection.
aide.start.step5: Check the stand opening schedule, then the staffing requirement. Both screens answer before any computation.
aide.start.step6: If your days are only described by an opening span, generate the split into vacations. With day templates, the grid is ready already.
aide.start.step7: Run a short solve, read the Problems page, fix, then run again over a long duration. Change only one thing at a time between two attempts.
aide.start.step8: Publish: only the people whose schedule has changed get a message. This is also the only moment subscribed calendars move.
aide.start.step9: Follow the acknowledgements on the Staff page, and turn on the nightly mailings on the Settings page to chase the silent ones.
aide.start.step10: Check that the schedule fair is open — it is by default — then close it once the schedule is frozen. On the day itself, event-day mode takes over.
aide.start.guichets: The counters open and close by hand, all on the Settings page, Edition tab, and they are the only places a staff member ever writes anything: the availability collection — and carpooling, which follows it — before the build, the schedule fair after publication. Each also accepts a dated period, but the switch stays in charge. The collection is closed until you open it; the fair is open by default.
aide.start.theme: Top right, a button cycles the display between automatic, light and dark. “Automatic” follows your device setting; an explicit choice pins the display on this browser.

aide.data.title: Reference data
aide.data.summary: What each reference screen describes, and the most common data-entry traps.
aide.data.def.animateurs: Identity, date of birth, skills per category with a level (beginner, autonomous, referent), unavailable days. The legal bracket — under 16, 16-18, adult — is never entered: it is recomputed at the date of each timeslot. A staff member is available by default, so only enter the absences: the shortest way is a click on the day, on the strip of their fiche; in the form, a click on a day of the strip marks it absent, and “Absent from” … “to” lays a range in one go. Levels are entered in bulk in the skills grid, which “Enter in the grid (row pre-filtered)” opens on the person. The “Age / regime” column gives the age on the first day of the edition. The name opens the person's fiche, which keeps the list's filter and sort for “Previous” and “Next”; “Filter” narrows the list to minors, managers, a skill or a wish, each filter staying shown above the table. Once a plan is computed, the “Seats” column counts each person's seats.
aide.data.def.stands: Categories offered, minimum and maximum simultaneous headcount, possible adults-only restriction, premium and effort markers, opening hours. “Add” guides the creation in four steps — identity, categories, location, hours: the edition's timeslots are offered open, you untick the ones the stand is closed on, type how many people it holds on each and untick the weekdays it does not open; no rule to write. The table sorts on every column; “Open” counts its open days and its seats, and “Coverage” appears once a schedule is computed. “Bulk edit” changes the ticked stands at once, or failing that every stand the table shows; “Enter as a grid”, “Import the grid” and “Compact the schedules” sit in the “More” menu. The name opens the stand's fiche: its day × timeslot grid is edited in place, as its row in the Stand hours grid — an empty cell closes, a block pastes from a spreadsheet, “Copy this day” lays a day on the others, Ctrl+D takes the day above —, then its opening anomalies, its seats after the solve (an empty seat opens in the seat panel of the Planning page), “Compare with…” and the history of its changes. “Edit the identity” shows the identity fields only. The folded “Rules” section gives the condensed form the grid saves — rules valid every day on one line such as “10:00-12:00, 14:00-”, special cases, dated exceptions, a window naming its own headcount “@2” — for whoever wants to read it or write it with “Edit the rules”.
aide.data.def.autres: A location is a geolocated place to attach a stand to: it avoids back-and-forth from one timeslot to the next. Locations are the “Locations” tab of the Stands page: a map shows them all with their stands, and dragging a marker there corrects its position without opening a record; the table, sortable at will, says which stands are attached to each. A stand's form offers “New location…” without leaving the page. A category is the shared vocabulary between a staff member's skills and a stand's games — without a shared category, the staff member cannot hold the stand. Also tick, in the “Ninja category” column of the Categories screen, the category whose holders are all-rounders: the solver tries to keep one of them free on every timeslot. Without it, that reserve does not exist.
aide.data.typologiesOrphelines: For each category, the Categories screen counts the staff members who master it (polyvalents aside), those who wished for it and the stands offering it; every figure leads to the list it counts, and the grid icon to that category's levels. An “Orphan” badge flags a category a stand offers and nobody masters: only a polyvalent can then hold that stand. “Fragile” means a single person, “Unused” no stand. Once a plan is computed, three columns say what it made of them: the seats, the hours, and the people “Assigned without the skill”. The edition status counts the orphans, before any solve.
aide.data.bulk: Every screen lets you tick several rows to delete or edit them in one go. In a bulk edit, a field left empty means “Leave unchanged”: the values specific to each row are preserved. This also applies to opening hours: a rule valid for twenty stands is entered once.
aide.importCsv.title: Staff CSV import
aide.importCsv.summary: Reuse your staff spreadsheet without retyping it: the tabs available, the format expected, and the two refusals that surprise you the first time.
aide.importCsv.colonnes: Skills, wishes and unavailable days hold several values in one cell, separated by “|”. A skill is written “category” or “category:REFERENT”; with no level, it counts as “autonomous”. Dates are read as DD/MM/YYYY as well as YYYY-MM-DD, but prefer the ISO form: a spreadsheet turns “12/09/2026” into “12/09/26”, which the import then reads as the most recent possible year — and the preview flags every date understood that way.
aide.importCsv.exemple: “Download an example file” gives a short CSV, ready to open in a spreadsheet: the eight columns read, filled with a dozen fictional people. It is the shortest way to see what a skills cell must look like. Its content comes from the demonstration scenario: copy its shape, not its values.
aide.data.copieHoraires: When several stands follow the same day, do not type it again. In a stand's form, “Copy the schedule of…” takes another stand's whole schedule, window headcounts included; nothing is saved before “Update stand”. In a bulk edit, “Replace with another stand’s” does the same across the selection. A copied window that exceeds the target stand's maximum headcount is flagged before saving.
aide.data.avertissements: Some entries are saved with a warning to read. The most frequent: an unavailability outside the event dates or on a day with no timeslot, a date of birth that makes the person a minor during the event, a timeslot no stand is open to cover, an opening window that overlaps no timeslot. An edit only flags what it changes, and as long as the edition has no timeslot these warnings stay silent.
aide.calculer.title: Calculate, fix, start over
aide.calculer.summary: The three ways to start the solver, and which one to pick.
aide.calculer.intro: The Solver page does not ask you to pick a mechanism, but to say what you want: the best schedule possible, a fix that moves as little as possible, or a blank page. All three read the same data and honour the same rules; what changes is where the computation starts from.
aide.calculer.def.calculer: The everyday button. If a schedule is saved, the computation starts from it and tries to improve it; otherwise it starts from scratch. Everything may move, planning locks apart, but on unchanged data the result cannot end below the starting plan. The line under the buttons says where the next computation will start from.
aide.calculer.def.corriger: A withdrawal, an unavailability entered late, a stand added: the schedule is already out and you want to move as little as possible. Everything still valid is frozen, only the seats the change invalidated are recomputed, in a few tens of seconds. The dialog first shows what changed since the plan, then offers to re-open more: animateurs, days, stands. The report names who moved. It re-optimises nothing.
aide.calculer.def.recommencer: Ignores the saved plan and starts from nothing. It is the only gesture that can lose the quality already reached, hence the confirmation: keep it for an attempt you are abandoning or for data rebuilt from the ground up. With no saved plan, the button is inactive.
aide.calculer.def.passeGestes: Manual gestures follow the same rule: moving an assignment on a day view, accepting a swap, applying or asking for a repair on a seat whose timeslot has already started is refused — “This timeslot has already started: the past no longer changes” — from the screen, the API or an assistant. Day-of mode keeps acting on the remaining timeslots of the day; the seat of a timeslot in progress stays as it is, the absence is merely recorded on it. With PASSE_FIGE=false, nothing is refused.
aide.calculer.def.rienAPlanifier: A computation launched while every timeslot has already started — the edition is over, or the simulated date is after the event — is refused instead of producing an empty schedule at zero hard; the job says so in its error. When past seats stayed empty (no recorded holder, for instance on the first computation launched during the event), the computation runs and the recap announces it: “N past seats stayed empty”.
aide.calculer.def.plancherPasse: The load and demanding-timeslot balances measure the whole edition, past seats included, and the computation can only move the future: a gap already dug before today cannot be caught up and leaves a medium score no computation will bring back to zero. This is expected, and it is why the score is compared from one computation to the next rather than to zero.
aide.calculer.verrous: Planning locks are not a fourth mode: they apply to all three. A locked staff member, stand, day or timeslot is touched neither by a full computation nor by a fix.
aide.config.title: Configuring the solver
aide.config.summary: The settings that change how the solver behaves, and which one to touch first.
aide.config.intro: The solver has no “quality level” to set: within the time it is given, it looks for the best schedule according to the active constraints. Settings therefore act either on the time granted, or on the rules to respect.
aide.config.def.duree: Set per edition on the Planning rules page, Solve tab, shared by every browser and applied by the server to every solve launched on the edition, from the screen as from the assistant. Two settings. The maximum duration (15 min by default) is the one that matters most: start short — 1 to 3 min — to reveal structural blockers, then move to 15 or 30 min, or more, for the final solve. The stop without improvement (5 min by default, 0 for never) cuts short a solve that no longer progresses; it only counts once the hard score is zero, so a solve never gives up while seats remain to fill. Both are bounded by a ceiling the instance's operator sets, shown above the fields: a value above it is refused. If the operator lowers that ceiling below a value already saved, the solve runs at the ceiling and says so. « Back to default » returns the edition to the instance's values, once saved.
aide.config.def.historique: A rule's panel, opened with a click on its name in Planning rules, shows every change of its weight or activation — value before and after, default included, date and origin: screen, assistant, scenario import or edition duplication — and, between two changes, the solves that followed with their score and the number of violations of that rule, as a dated list and a small chart. Putting the same value back writes nothing. It is a juxtaposition, not a measure of effect: the reference data may have changed between two solves. The history belongs to the edition and disappears with it; a duplicated edition starts with the dosage inherited from its source, not with its source's history.
aide.config.def.legaux: On the Planning rules page, Legal tab, each on the row of the rule that reads it: the weekly caps on the weekly durations, the length of the legal break on the durations and continuous work, the meal window and length on the meal break. The caps (48 h for adults, 35 h for minors) are ordre public: a higher value is refused, a lower one stays free. The break lasts at least 20 minutes (art. L3121-16), raised to 30 for a minor (art. L3162-3), 30 by default. The minimum daily rest (11 h, 9 h by collective agreement) and the maximum length of a shift, which only the grid check reads, are set under the table. Nothing requires a gap between two shifts.
aide.config.def.contraintes: Every rule of the catalogue is switched off on its row of the Planning rules page, then “Save”. Use it to diagnose — “without this rule, does the schedule become feasible?” — far more than to produce: switching off a hard constraint produces a schedule reality will refuse. Switching off a soft rule that measures nothing, for want of data entered, does make the score readable without changing the result.
aide.adHoc.title: Manual adjustments
aide.adHoc.summary: Force, forbid, bring together: what each type covers, and the edge cases that surprise.
aide.adHoc.intro: A manual adjustment is an exception you enter on your own data, alongside the rules of the catalogue — first tab of the Instructions to the solver page, with the locks and the consignes. Three of the four types are applied at the same level as the legal framework: the solver will never work around them, even if it means returning a schedule at fault. Each is entered with a reason, readable wherever the adjustment is cited.
aide.adHoc.callout.title: Manual adjustment or lock?
aide.adHoc.callout.text: Both take freedom away from the solver, but not at the same moment. A manual adjustment is a made-to-measure rule, set before the computation, saying where to place or not to place someone: “she cannot come on Sunday”, “these two do not work together”. The solver honours it on every solve, including one starting from scratch. A planning lock is a gesture on a plan already computed: it freezes what a solve produced so the next one leaves it alone; it says nothing about what ought to be there, and never freezes an empty place. In practice: to impose or forbid an assignment, an adjustment; to protect a part you have validated, a lock.
aide.adHoc.def.indisponibilite: Forbids the person to hold a seat within the chosen scope. Not to be confused with the unavailable days on their record, which cover a whole day: here you target a precise timeslot, a precise stand, or both.
aide.adHoc.def.affectation: Requires at least one seat of the scope to be held by that person. Careful: if you name several staff members, the adjustment is satisfied as soon as one of them holds the seat — it means "any one of these", never "all of them". To require two people, enter two adjustments.
aide.adHoc.def.incompatibilite: Forbids two people to work on the same timeslot. It bears on the timeslot, not on the stand: two different stands at the same hour are just as forbidden. Only the first two staff members of the list are taken into account — for three people, enter the three pairs.
aide.adHoc.def.affinite: Not a hard rule: a preference, rewarded every time both people hold a seat on the same stand on the same timeslot. It forces nothing.
aide.adHoc.perimetre: The timeslot and the stand are optional, and leaving them empty means “everywhere”: a forced unavailability with no scope keeps the person off the whole event. An adjustment keeps the identifier of the timeslot it targets — if that timeslot disappears, the Scope column shows “deleted time slot” and the adjustment no longer applies to anything. After a split or a calendar application, check the ones that targeted a timeslot.
aide.adHoc.contradictions: Two adjustments that cannot hold together are refused on save, with a message naming both — rather than a schedule declared infeasible several minutes later. Five situations are refused:
aide.adHoc.refus1: the same pair declared both incompatible and in affinity;
aide.adHoc.refus2: a forced assignment whose whole scope is covered by a forced unavailability targeting every staff member it names;
aide.adHoc.refus3: two forced assignments pinning the same person on scopes that overlap in time;
aide.adHoc.refus4: two forced assignments placing two people declared incompatible on one time slot;
aide.adHoc.limites: The check only refuses what is certainly impossible, so as never to cost you a legitimate entry. What deliberately gets through: a forced assignment naming two staff members of whom only one is unavailable, an unavailability narrower than the forced scope, and two forced assignments on the same timeslot of which only one names a stand. Those combinations can still lead to a schedule at fault: the solve will settle it.
aide.adHoc.chevauchement: The overlap is computed on the timeslot hours as entered, not on what a stand closure actually leaves of them. Two forced assignments on timeslots that overlap, but on two stands closed at complementary hours, will therefore be refused. In that case, target timeslots that do not overlap.
aide.adHoc.intenable: Three other situations are flagged without being refused, because what breaks a forced assignment usually arrives after it: every staff member it names has declared the whole scope off; no seat of the scope can take them under a hard rule — a minor at night, on a public holiday, on an adults-only stand, past a daily cap; their schedule is locked over the whole scope without any of them already holding a seat there. A message says so when you save, the Problems page carries it as a blocking cause for as long as it stands, and « Calculer » asks for confirmation before starting.
aide.adHoc.modifier: Editing an adjustment means saving it again under its own identifier: the new version replaces the previous one, and that case is never refused as contradicting itself. An adjustment saved before this check existed, or imported, may however survive: the Problems page then reports it as a blocking cause, and the screen marks the rows concerned.
aide.adHoc.import: On importing a scenario, the adjustments in the file replace those of the edition wholesale: a file carrying none installs none. The export, for its part, writes the section as soon as the edition carries any. A file whose adjustments contradict each other is refused entirely.
aide.adHoc.apres: When a solve nonetheless ends at fault, the Problems page names the adjustments the solver could not honour, with the number of gaps each carries — that is what tells “the solver cannot manage” from “these three exceptions need arbitrating”.
aide.config.def.adhoc: Exceptions entered case by case, with a traced reason: forced unavailability, incompatibility, forced assignment. They are treated at the same level as hard constraints, so never worked around — and each one takes options away from the solver. A badly set adjustment blocks a schedule as surely as a shortage of staff.
aide.config.def.verrouillages: Freeze a staff member, a stand, a day or a timeslot so the next solve leaves it alone and optimises the rest. An unfilled seat is never frozen, and frozen seats keep being evaluated: a lock therefore leaves an alert visible rather than hiding a problem — and when what you freeze already breaks a hard rule, saving it says so, so the next run's negative hard score is no surprise. They are laid on the Locks tab of the Instructions to the solver page, on an animateur by default; before saving, the preview counts the assignments the lock will freeze and leads to the Day page that shows them. It is not a manual adjustment — see the “Manual adjustment or lock?” box.
aide.config.lock: One solve at a time runs for the whole server, possibly started from another machine; the toolbar monitor says which one and for how long. Only the edition the computation was started from is locked for data entry: on another one, you keep working.
aide.results.title: Reading and interpreting the results
aide.results.summary: The score, the feasibility banner, the Problems page: what each one says, and which to believe.
aide.results.score: A solve returns a three-part score, of the form “0hard / -6675medium / -120soft”. They never offset one another: the solver always prefers a schedule better on hard, whatever the price paid elsewhere.
aide.results.courbe: During the solve, the Solver page plots the three parts live, each in its own frame. The top of a frame is zero: a curve sticking to it means “nothing left to fix at that level”. When hard has been at zero for several minutes and soft no longer moves, the solve has plateaued: “Stop solver” will cost you nothing, a stopped solver still saves and analyses what it found. Only the running solve is plotted.
aide.results.def.hard: The only part to look at first. At zero, the schedule is valid: every place filled, no unavailability or missing skill, and the whole legal framework respected. Negative, the schedule cannot be used as it is.
aide.results.def.medium: What must be honoured as far as possible and reported otherwise: a referent per stand, load balancing, supervision of minors. A very negative medium does not invalidate the schedule, it signals degraded comfort.
aide.results.def.soft: What separates two valid schedules: stand rotation, mixing skill levels, fair sharing of demanding time slots. Never optimise it before the hard score is zero.
aide.results.previousPlan: A computation started again departs from the saved plan and cannot end below it on unchanged data. It can still degrade it if the reference data changed meanwhile, or if you started from scratch. The Solver page therefore shows the score before next to the one after and flags a worse solve — hard still at zero does not mean nothing was lost, the gap reads on medium. “Go back to the previous plan” restores the earlier schedule; do not wait, only the last five automatic snapshots are kept per edition.
aide.results.instantanes: One schedule is saved at a time, and every solve overwrites the previous one: it is the Snapshots page that keeps the others. A capture is taken there automatically before every solve. A plan you want to keep is set aside explicitly, with a label: that one is never purged, and serves as the term of comparison for the A/B comparator. Restoring during a solve is refused by the server: the solve would overwrite the plan you have just put back.
aide.results.def.faisabilite: A capacity estimate computed without solving, at the top of the Solver and Planning rules pages, naming the timeslots and stands at fault. It is optimistic: it ignores the split into vacations and the legal framework for minors, so it may announce as “feasible” a schedule the solver will not bring to zero. The reverse does not happen: if it reports a capacity shortfall, the shortfall is real.
aide.results.def.problemes: The complete, ranked list of causes. It mixes two sources: structural infeasibilities, computed without solving and visible as soon as the data is entered (insufficient capacity over a stretch, a category nobody masters, an adults-only stand with no adult available), and the rules at fault in the latest analysis. Every line points to the screen where to fix it. It is the first screen to open when a solve does not reach zero, and a good reflex even before running the first one.
aide.results.def.contraintes: The catalogue of rules in three tabs — Legal, Quality, Solve —, each on a row with its basis, its state, its settings and the result of the latest analysis: how many times it is not honoured, and the detail of the gaps in its panel. That is what turns “-14 hard” into “fourteen unfilled seats on such a stand”.
aide.results.def.stabilite: Once a schedule is published, every person moved off a seat they held costs one medium point: a computation started again after a late change only disturbs people already notified if the gain is worth the trouble. The rule is dosed like the others and stays silent as long as nothing has been published. It is not a freeze: for that, there are planning locks.
aide.results.def.pourquoiLui: A click on an assigned staff member explains that precise assignment: the rules honoured or not for that seat, in the seat panel of the Planning page. On request, the screen also looks for who could replace them, and only offers replacements that introduce no hard gap, each with its effect on the score. The search is bounded and says how many candidates it evaluated: a short list does not prove nothing else exists.
aide.tuning.title: Tuning the configuration
aide.tuning.summary: Symptom by symptom: what to change, and in which order.
aide.tuning.order: Always tune in this order: the data first, then the solving duration, and only last the constraints. Disabling a rule is a diagnostic tool, not a production method.
aide.tuning.def.postesVides: Look at the staffing requirement first: if the staff entered is below the estimated minimum, you are short of people, not of computation time. Otherwise, the Problems page says which timeslots are concerned — often a handful of peak timeslots, a stand opened by mistake, or a category almost nobody masters.
aide.tuning.term.plateau: The hard score stalls near zero
aide.tuning.def.plateau: This is the typical case where a longer duration pays: double it and run again. If two long solves stop at exactly the same score, the problem is no longer time but structure — identify the rule at fault and look at its gaps one by one.
aide.tuning.term.legal: The gaps are about working time
aide.tuning.def.legal: The weekly caps and the rest between days collide with the grid. Revisit the grid rather than the legal caps. When a stretch of more than six hours blocks, the answer is almost always one more place on the stand at break time, or a gap in the grid — not a raised cap.
aide.tuning.def.mineurs: The framework for minors is stricter and depends on their age at the date of the timeslot: no night work, a reduced daily span, longer breaks, two consecutive rest days, mandatory supervision by an adult. Check the dates of birth and the share of adults available on late timeslots.
aide.tuning.term.adhoc: The schedule became infeasible after a change
aide.tuning.def.adhoc: Look at the manual adjustments and planning locks added since the last successful solve: they carry the weight of a hard constraint. Remove the latest addition temporarily and run again to confirm. If two adjustments plainly contradict each other, the Problems page names them with no solve at all.
aide.tuning.term.mediumEleve: The medium or soft score looks huge
aide.tuning.def.mediumEleve: Check first that it is not a floor caused by missing data — wishes, referent level. Enriching skills and wishes improves those parts far more than any solver setting.
aide.tuning.method: Change only one thing at a time between two solves, and always run over the same duration so the scores stay comparable. The number of seats shown at the top of the Solver page lets you check that a data change had the effect you expected, before even running again.
aide.views.title: Browsing the schedule
aide.views.summary: Each view answers a different question; picking the right one saves time.
aide.views.def.day: One day as a table across the whole width: one stand per row, its location under its name, one timeslot per column, one name per label and each empty seat in red. A stand closed on a timeslot says so in grey, and a partial opening simply gives its hours. A stand's name leads to its profile. This is where you fix things by hand: a click on a name or on a “free seat” opens the seat panel on the right (see Seat panel below), which explains the seat and carries every gesture. “Move to…” is always offered there: pick the free seat to go to or the person to swap with; the server simulates the gesture and refuses it, naming the rule, if it would break a hard rule, and a locked seat does not move. If your instance has also switched drag and drop on, still being trialled, a name can also be dragged, by the handle on its left, onto another stand of the day — on a free seat the person moves, on a person the two swap. Drag and drop is off by default: it only governs that mouse gesture, never the move itself.
aide.views.def.repartitionHeures: The second rendering of “By stand”: what weighs in the edition, in one picture. Each rectangle is a stand, its area the seat-hours to staff over the period — filled and empty seats alike, over the seat's real window: a person's break does not reduce their stand's need. Its colour says how much of those hours is actually held, on thresholds of its own: critical under 80 %, hatched as well as red, partial up to 99 %, staffed at 100 % — the grid, for its part, calls empty only a cell nobody holds. Stands are grouped by location, or by typologie: a stand offering several typologies is filed once, under their combination (“Ambiance + Stratégie”), so the areas add up to the edition's total — the By typologie axis, for its part, counts a seat once per typologie. When one group crushes the others, the smallest are gathered under “Others”. The page's Location filter applies to it. A click zooms into a group, the breadcrumb takes you back, and a click on a stand opens its day, by day. The table folded under the picture gives the same figures, 0 h stands included. Overstaffing does not show: the schedule creates no seat beyond the need.
aide.views.def.hours: The estimated minimum number of people to recruit — each person's hours are on “By person”. It is computed before any solve, from the stands and timeslots alone: four bounds, the largest of which is kept — the peak of simultaneous seats, that peak extended by the legal break, the load of the heaviest week, and the rotation over days. Each is a proven floor, never a target. It also reads typologie by typologie: a typologie whose minimum exceeds the number of people who declare it is the bottleneck.

aide.exchange.summary: Getting data in, getting schedules out, and diagnosing the rest.
aide.exchange.item.csvAnimateurs: Staff CSV import: reuse your spreadsheet without retyping it. The expected format has its own section in this guide.
aide.exchange.item.sql: Exporting and importing a full SQL dump, to duplicate or restore an entire data set.

The list is built from the repository's history, so nobody keeps it up to date and it cannot lie about what is running. « Worth watching » first flags the changes that deserve a check before the next solve.
aide.historique.title: Action history
aide.historique.summary: Who did what in this edition, and what was refused.
aide.historique.intro: The page scrolls, newest first, through what was done in the current edition: the time, the action, the object, the fields an edit actually changed, and the author. It is the page to open when a piece of data changed and nobody remembers touching it. A refused action appears there too, marked “refused”: that is often the line you are after — an import that wrote nothing, a publication attempted during a solve, an expired espace link.
aide.historique.def.acteurs: “Administration”: someone signed in to the administration. “Staff”: an action from an espace. “Unidentified”: a call with no valid credential, a wrong or expired espace link — those lines are refusals. “Assistant”: a call from MCP. “Application”: the nightly tasks. Each family has its filter button, and “Completed / Refused” filters separately.
aide.historique.term.contenu: What a line does not say
aide.historique.def.contenu: No values: “name, e-mail” says what moved, never what it became. The history is not a backup and does not let you go back — that is what snapshots are for. No identity either: the line keeps an identifier, so a record deleted since leaves a line that names nobody. What is traced is writes and data going out — exports, dumps, e-mails — never reads, nor computations that write nothing.
aide.historique.def.portee: The last two hundred actions of the edition you are on, and the filters work on those: a search that returns nothing therefore does not prove the action never happened, only that it has left that window. “Exports” is the exception: the server then looks for the last two hundred files taken out over the whole period kept, however many changes happened since. Beyond it, a retention bounds the table — ninety days by default, set by the operator. A log you can edit is not a log: no button on this screen erases anything.
aide.historique.filtres: Five filters combine: free search, object, author, outcome and “Exports”. They stay in the page address, so in a link you send. A common case: a staff record that is no longer what you thought — filter on the object “ANIMATEUR” and type its identifier, the line says when, by whom, and which fields changed. “Exports” keeps only the files that left the application — exports from the administration, the database dump, schedules downloaded from an espace: it answers “who took the staff list out, and when?”, and “did they actually get their schedule?”.
aide.mcp.title: Driving the application from an assistant (MCP)
aide.mcp.summary: Plug an AI assistant onto the edition to read and change it — with a key that opens everything.
aide.mcp.intro: MCP is the protocol an assistant uses to talk to an application. Plugged onto this one, it answers in plain language — “how many empty seats on Saturday afternoon?”, “start a solve again” — and it really acts: it goes through the same services as the screens, with the same checks and the same refusals. The MCP page gives the endpoint and the configuration to paste into the client.
aide.mcp.def.cle: It is set on the server by the operator, not from this screen. While it does not exist, MCP refuses everyone and the page says so. When it does, “Reveal the API key” shows it after confirming the administrator password, then hides it after two minutes or as soon as you leave the page.
aide.mcp.def.pouvoir: Everything the administration does, writing included: creating and deleting data, starting a solve, publishing, emptying an edition. It belongs to nobody and does not expire: treat it as a password and have it replaced at the slightest doubt. An assistant plugged onto it acts with no on-screen confirmation — before letting it touch a real edition, take a snapshot.
aide.mcp.def.donnees: No surname, first name, date of birth or e-mail address. An assistant designates a person by their staff identifier, and knows nothing of them beyond their planning attributes and their bracket — minor, under sixteen, adult — inferred from the date without the date travelling. An answer given as identifiers is read back on the Staff page, whose filter accepts them.
aide.mcp.def.proxy: When the application is published behind an access proxy, the page detects it and says so: every call must then also present a proxy token, which the proposed configuration already carries. A detail that costs half an hour when overlooked: the key goes in its own header, never in “Authorization”, which a proxy often consumes for itself.
aide.mcp.def.prompts: The server announces a dozen ready-made requests of its own: checking that an edition is ready, diagnosing the hard constraints still violated, restarting a solve without losing the plan in place, processing declarations, publishing. A client that handles MCP prompts offers them directly; otherwise, “Copy the prompt”.
aide.mcp.journal: Nothing an assistant writes is invisible: every write leaves a line in the action history, under the author “Assistant”.

aide.foire.title: Schedule swap fair (shift swaps)
aide.foire.summary: Staff propose their swaps themselves; nothing is applied without your approval.
aide.foire.intro: Every staff member has a personal espace, opened by a link of their own. No account to create, but a code sent to the e-mail address on their record is asked for once per device: the schedule is downloaded from the espace, so a minimum of authentication is called for. Someone with no address cannot get in — add one.
aide.foire.def.espace: They build their list of requests then submit it in one go. When they have nobody in mind, “who can replace me?” looks for the colleagues with whom the swap actually holds. They then follow the status of each one, with your comment, and can cancel while nothing is decided. The link to their espace is copied — and regenerated, if a PDF has leaked — from their record on the Staff page.
aide.foire.def.planPublie: A staff member's espace shows the plan that was sent to them, not the one you are working on: an approved swap, a replacement or a new solve only move their espace once published. As long as nothing has been published, the espaces stay empty and say so. Publishing is refused during a solve.
aide.foire.def.abonnement: A staff member can give their calendar a permanent subscription address instead of downloading an ICS that goes stale. What the calendar re-reads on every sync is the published schedule: “my calendar is not updating” therefore almost always means the change has not been published yet. That address is a second credential, distinct from the espace link: regenerating the link does not cut off their subscription, and the person replaces their own address if it leaks. You never see it.
aide.foire.def.ouverture: The fair's switch, on the Settings page, Edition tab, Counters card, opens or closes it for the current edition; it is open by default. The Swaps screen keeps a one-line state of it, with a button to close it. Closed, the espaces go read-only: the schedule stays visible and downloadable, but no request is accepted any more, and the refusal comes from the server. You can also bound the fair with two dates — the switch stays in charge. Before the opening date, the espace says “not open yet” and gives the date to come back on, never “closed”.
aide.foire.def.ecran: The pending requests, each with its measured impact: a cross swap or a plain take-over, the effect on the score, the hard rules that would break. Accepting applies the swap immediately, exactly as simulated, and locks it on its timeslot: a later solve will not undo it. Refusing changes nothing, and the reason is passed to the staff member. A decided request stays marked “not communicated yet” until you have published.
aide.foire.def.envoi: The “Publish” button on the Publication page carries its count: “Publish — 3 people concerned”. It only writes to the staff whose schedule has changed since the last publication, and the message says what changes for each. Ten fixes in a row therefore do not make ten e-mails: they fill a queue you empty when you are done. The report names the staff with no address and the failed mailings. On a large headcount, sending takes several tens of seconds.
aide.foire.term.relecture: Read the list over before sending
aide.foire.def.relecture: « See who is concerned » opens one line per person: what changes for them, their last confirmation, and a ticked box. Sort by size of change to start with the biggest ones, fold away the minor changes — same stand, a quarter of an hour of drift at most — and export the whole thing as CSV to read it over elsewhere. The filter decides nothing: the folded rows go out all the same.
aide.foire.def.differer: Untick somebody and their message is deferred, not lost: they receive nothing, and the next publication names them again with the gap accumulated since their last message — the one they really received, not the plan published in between. This is the « I will call them first » move. Unticking everybody is refused: publishing without notifying anyone would make no sense.
aide.editions.variante: Duplicating an edition copies stands, opening hours, staff and their current unavailabilities, but neither the assignments nor the espace links — a link always designates exactly one edition.
aide.editions.rituel1: The day before: duplicate the current edition (“2026” → “2026-heatwave”).

aide.rappels.title: Acknowledgements and reminders
aide.rappels.summary: Know who has read their schedule, and let the application chase the others — once.
aide.rappels.intro: Once the schedule is published, every staff member sees a “I have read it and I will be there” button in their espace. The “Acknowledgement” column on the Staff page gives you the answer, and the table filter accepts “confirmed”, “chased” or “silent”.
aide.rappels.def.statuts: “Silent”: nothing came back. “Confirmed”: the button was clicked, the date shows on hover. “Chased”: the reminder went out and is still unanswered. Someone with no seat at all in the published schedule shows “—”: nothing was asked of them, they do not count among the people to chase.
aide.rappels.def.republication: A new publication only asks for a confirmation again from the people whose schedule actually changed. Someone merely told of a swap decision reads the same days as before: asking them again would turn the button into a reflex rather than an answer.
aide.rappels.def.activation: Nightly mailings are off until you turn them on, edition by edition, on the Settings page, Edition tab. It is the only safeguard: a past edition carries the same records, and nothing tells this year's staff from last year's. Duplicating an edition does not copy that setting.
aide.rappels.def.delais: The send time of the day-before reminder (6 p.m. by default, 11 p.m. at the latest: the task runs once an hour, and a reminder set later would never go out), the silence tolerated after a publication before chasing, and the age of a swap request that triggers an alert. All three are set per edition.
aide.rappels.def.relance: Past the delay, the silent ones get a confirmation reminder and move to “Chased”. They will get no other: chasing someone every evening does not make them answer faster. The last few are yours to take in hand.
aide.rappels.def.relanceManuelle: On the eve of the event, one more night is one too many. On the Staff page, the “Acknowledgements” filter isolates the people never confirmed or silent for N days; select them and “Remind now” sends them the same reminder the night would. The rule does not change: one chaser per person and per publication, and the report names those it left out.
aide.rappels.silence: “I got nothing” almost always has the same cause: the edition was never armed. Then comes a schedule never published, then records with no e-mail address. These alerts close by dealing with what they report, not by clearing them.
espace.aide.confirmer.question: What does “I have read it and I will be there” mean?
espace.aide.confirmer.resume: One click telling the organisers you have seen your schedule.
espace.aide.confirmer.pourquoi: The button appears as soon as your schedule is published. One click is enough: the organisers see that you know, and do not have to chase you. With no answer after a few days, an automatic reminder goes out — once only.
espace.aide.confirmer.deuxFois: Clicking twice changes nothing: the first date is the one that counts, and the button then gives way to “Attendance confirmed on…”.
espace.aide.confirmer.republication: If the organisers publish a new version and your days change, the question is put to you again. If nothing moved for you, your confirmation stands.
espace.aide.confirmer.probleme: Confirming does not bind you for good, and it is not the place to report a problem. If a timeslot does not work, use the Swaps tab or contact the organisers.
espace.aide.veille.question: Will I get a reminder before the event?
espace.aide.veille.resume: The evening before, an e-mail lists your assignments for the next day.
espace.aide.veille.contenu: If the organisers have turned reminders on, you get the list of your timeslots for the next day on the evening before: time and stand, nothing more. It is what this page already shows — a reminder never announces a change.
espace.aide.veille.absence: No reminder? Three possible reasons: your record has no e-mail address, the organisers have not turned reminders on, or you are assigned nowhere that day. Either way, this page stays the reference.
animateurs.confirmation.aide:

• Reminded: a single reminder, at night or by hand.
• —: no assignment in the published schedule.

aide.setup.intro: A schedule that does not fill up is rarely a matter of computation time. Three causes come back, in this order: a need badly described, a grid of timeslots that forces two teams where one would do, and settings that say more than the law does.
aide.setup.term.stands: A headcount per window, not per stand
aide.setup.def.stands: The stand's minimum headcount applies to the whole day. If a stand is held by two in the morning and four in the afternoon, entering “2” under-staffs the afternoon and entering “4” over-staffs the morning. Give every opening window its headcount, and leave empty the ones that fall back on the minimum. On a meal-relay vacation, half that headcount is required, rounded up.
aide.setup.term.ouvertures: Check what the solver will read
aide.setup.def.ouvertures: The “Stand hours” grid shows, stand by slot, the resolved headcounts and the seats they generate. A stand never open, a window outside the timeslots, a stretch too short to be a shift show there before any computation. A stand nobody needs to staff at a given hour is declared closed, never at headcount zero.
aide.setup.term.creneaux: Blocks, and what a cut costs
aide.setup.def.creneaux: The solver assigns one person per timeslot and per seat. Vacations that touch chain freely: nothing requires a gap between two of them, and a gap shorter than the legal break counts as work. Still prefer blocks — morning, midday, afternoon, evening — and keep the midday changeover as a planned gap: that is the lunch break. Splitting an afternoon in two never reduces how many people you need.
aide.setup.term.pause: The legal break: a gap, or a relay
aide.setup.def.pause: The Code du travail imposes a break from six hours in a row (four and a half for a minor). The tool recognises it two ways, and no third: a gap of at least the configured length in the grid — it splits the stretch, nothing more is owed — or a relay, a colleague of the same stand holding a place for the whole break. A break nobody can take is a hard gap.
aide.setup.term.surPoste: A changeover chained to the afternoon is still possible
aide.setup.def.surPoste: A 1 p.m. to 8 p.m. stint is seven hours in a row: it owes a break around the sixth hour, and it is legal as soon as a colleague holds the stand at that moment. Nothing to declare: open the place, the solver uses it. The Breaks screen then lays out the rotation, one person at a time per stand, and names the days where the relay is missing. A break is rest, so the caps and every hours counter deduct it.
aide.setup.term.coupureRepas: The meal break, a rule of its own
aide.setup.def.coupureRepas: It is not the legal break, and a relay does not lift it. Anyone working on both sides of a meal window must have, entirely inside that window, a free gap of the required length. Starting your stint when the window opens, or ending it when it closes, owes nothing. Worth knowing before splitting: if a single timeslot covers the whole window, the person holding it cannot step away, and no solve will reach zero hard gap until the grid is recut.
aide.setup.term.repos: Weekly rest, read in one stretch
aide.setup.def.repos: Thirty-five consecutive hours a week is twenty-four hours plus the daily rest. A rest taken on Sunday or Monday straddles the change of week: it counts whole for the week it falls in. On an event open seven days a week, that is what makes one rest day per person per week possible.
aide.setup.term.contraintes: Switch none of them off to fill up
aide.setup.def.contraintes: Six days a week, ten hours a day, eleven hours of daily rest, forty-eight hours a week are the law. Switching off a legal rule serves to understand what blocks, never to produce the schedule you send out. Comfort rules do not prevent a complete schedule: they rank it.
aide.setup.step1: Staffing requirement: the bounds give the floor. Below the floor, no setting will change anything.
aide.setup.step2: Stand hours, then feasibility: the need window by window, the capacity day by day, with no computation.
aide.setup.step3: A short solve, then the Problems page: the remaining gaps say which rule is holding the seats empty.
aide.setup.step4: A long solve, once the configuration is stable, changing only one thing at a time.
aide.setup.step5: Fragility, then Breaks: who is irreplaceable, and which relays to organise before publishing.
aide.setup.repere: One yardstick for arbitrating: a grid with a lower headcount bound does not necessarily solve better. The bound says what is impossible, never what is feasible — only the solve settles it.

cgu.objet.title: Purpose
cgu.objet.texte: This application helps an event's organisation build, share and adjust the schedule of its animateurs. It is made available by the organisation named in the legal notice, for its own needs and those of the people it schedules. Using it — as an administrator or from an animateur's personal space — constitutes acceptance of these terms.
cgu.aideDecision.title: The tool assists the decision, it does not make it
cgu.aideDecision.texte: The application computes schedule proposals from the data entered: stands, timeslots, availability, skills, and the configured working-time rules. That computation is a {$START_TAG_STRONG}decision aid{$CLOSE_TAG_STRONG}. It amounts to neither legal validation, nor certification of compliance, nor any commitment as to whether a schedule is actually workable.
cgu.aideDecision.humain: No schedule is applied without having been reviewed and approved by the organisation, which may correct it, impose or forbid an assignment. Likewise, no swap request is applied without its explicit decision.
cgu.aideDecision.limites: The results depend entirely on the accuracy of the data entered and the parameters chosen. A wrong date of birth, an undeclared unavailability or a badly set hourly ceiling produce a schedule the application will deem valid and which will not be.

espace.aide.sousTitre: Everything you can do from your space: read your schedule, take it with you, and request a timeslot swap. Open the question that concerns you.
espace.aide.espace.question: What is this space for?
espace.aide.espace.resume: To read your schedule, always up to date, and to ask for a swap.
espace.aide.espace.intro: The organisers spread the staff across the stands, timeslot by timeslot. This espace is your own view: your timeslots, and nothing else.
espace.aide.espace.item1: See your timeslots day by day, with the stand and your teammates.
espace.aide.espace.item2: Take your schedule with you as a PDF or in your phone's calendar.
espace.aide.espace.item3: Ask to swap a timeslot, as long as the schedule fair is open.
espace.aide.espace.item4: Answer the swap requests a colleague sends you.
espace.aide.espace.limite: You never change the schedule yourself: everything goes through a request the organisers approve.
espace.aide.acces.question: How do I get into my space?
espace.aide.acces.resume: Through your personal link, then a code sent by e-mail.
espace.aide.acces.intro: The link the organisers sent you is personal: it opens your schedule and only yours. The first time you open it on a device, a 6-digit code is sent to the e-mail address the organisers have. It is valid for 10 minutes, and you get 5 tries.
espace.aide.acces.item1: One code per device. Once entered, that device stays signed in for about a month, then a new code is asked for.
espace.aide.acces.item2: Code not received? Look in your spam folder, then ask for a new one.
espace.aide.acces.item3: Do not forward your link: whoever opens it sees your schedule.
espace.aide.acces.item4: “This link is no longer valid”, or no e-mail address on your record: contact the organisers.
espace.aide.planning.question: How do I read my schedule?
espace.aide.planning.resume: One card per day; on each line, the hours, the stand and your teammates.
espace.aide.planning.def.horaire: The start and end of your timeslot. You are expected at the start time, not when the stand opens.
espace.aide.planning.def.stand: The game or post you hold. It can change from one timeslot to the next within the same day.
espace.aide.planning.def.lieu: Where the stand is set up, when it has a place — “Hall B”, “Castle”. If it is on a map, the name is a link that opens it.
espace.aide.planning.def.coequipiers: The staff on the same stand, on the same timeslot as you.
espace.aide.planning.def.pause: As soon as your day reaches six hours in a row, you are entitled to a twenty-minute break. Your schedule tells you from when to when to take it. Breaks on the same stand follow one another, one person at a time: step out at the stated time, or ask the organisers for a relay if you are alone.
espace.aide.planning.repos: Days where you are assigned nowhere still show, marked “Rest”. That is on purpose: nothing has been forgotten.
espace.aide.planning.maj: “Schedule communicated on…” tells you how old the version you are reading is. It only changes when the organisers publish again, and you are then told by e-mail. Still, come back here before you set off: this page is what counts.
espace.aide.planning.changements: After a republication that concerns you, the “What changed for you” banner repeats, above your days, what the message said — handy if you missed it. It is collapsed, with the number of changes in its title; tap it to read. It clears once you have confirmed you will be there.
espace.aide.planning.maintenant: During the event, the page opens on today: at the top, your current or next seat, and the break you still have to take. Past days are folded behind “See past days”. A seat running past midnight stays shown as current until it ends.
espace.aide.planning.vide: If nothing shows, the schedule has not been published yet. Nothing to do on your side.
espace.aide.emporter.question: Can I take my schedule with me?
espace.aide.emporter.resume: Yes — best of all by subscribing to it, so that it keeps itself up to date.
espace.aide.emporter.item0: “Subscribe in my calendar” — the one to prefer: given once to your calendar, the address keeps it up to date on every new publication. Nothing to redo afterwards.
espace.aide.emporter.item1: “PDF booklet”: an overview of your days, their detail, then your team-mates and your places.
espace.aide.emporter.item2: “ICS file”: each timeslot becomes an appointment, poured into your calendar once.
espace.aide.emporter.photo: The PDFs and the ICS are a snapshot taken at download time: they do not update themselves when the schedule changes or a swap is approved. At the slightest doubt, trust this page.
espace.aide.emporter.itemFeuille: “A4 sheet”: the same schedule on a single sheet, a calendar on the front, teams and places on the back — the one that fits in a pocket.
espace.aide.emporter.qr: Both PDFs carry a QR code: scan it off the paper to come back here instead of retyping the address.
espace.aide.emporter.abonnement: At the top of “My schedule”, the “Take my schedule with me” band offers four ways out.
espace.aide.emporter.abonnementColler: Some applications, Google Calendar first of all, want the address pasted rather than clicked. It is then under "Copy the address, or replace it", in the same band.
espace.aide.emporter.abonnementPrudence: That address is personal: whoever gets it sees your schedule, with no code or password. Do not put it on a shared calendar. If it gets out, “This address leaked, replace it” creates a new one and cuts the old one off at once.
espace.aide.echange.question: How do I request a swap?
espace.aide.echange.resume: From “My swaps”: build your list of requests, then submit it.
espace.aide.echange.step1: Pick the timeslot you want to be freed from.
espace.aide.echange.step2: Pick the colleague to swap with.
espace.aide.echange.step3: To take one of their timeslots in return, name it. Without that choice, the swap only covers yours.
espace.aide.echange.step4: Give a reason: this is what the organisers will read to decide.
espace.aide.echange.step5: “Add to the list”, then start over if several timeslots are involved.
espace.aide.echange.step6: “Submit my requests”: nothing leaves before that button.
espace.aide.echange.brouillon: Until you submit, the list is only a draft: the cross removes a request, and nobody has received anything yet.
espace.aide.remplacants.question: I have nobody in mind, what now?
espace.aide.remplacants.resume: “Who can replace me?” finds the swaps that work for you.
espace.aide.remplacants.intro: Once your timeslot is picked, this button goes through your colleagues and only keeps the swaps compatible with the rest of the schedule and with the rest rules. The proposals come in three families:
espace.aide.remplacants.term.libere: Someone frees you from this timeslot
espace.aide.remplacants.def.libere: A colleague takes it over, and you are off duty at that time.
espace.aide.remplacants.term.dirige: You trade it for another timeslot
espace.aide.remplacants.def.dirige: You leave them yours and take one of theirs, at another moment.
espace.aide.remplacants.term.croise: You swap on that same timeslot
espace.aide.remplacants.def.croise: You stay on duty at the same hours, but on another stand.
espace.aide.remplacants.limite: The list shows the most promising leads, not all of them. If nothing comes up, you can still propose the swap to someone: the organisers will decide.
espace.aide.suivi.question: What happens to my request?
espace.aide.suivi.resume: It goes through your colleague's agreement, then through the organisers' decision.
espace.aide.suivi.intro: Each request carries a chip saying where it stands:
espace.aide.suivi.def.attenteCible: Your colleague has to agree first.
espace.aide.suivi.def.proposee: The agreement is given; the organisers still have to decide.
espace.aide.suivi.def.acceptee: The swap is approved. It appears in your schedule at the next publication: as long as the old timeslot is showing, it has not happened yet — the request says so under its status.
espace.aide.suivi.def.refusee: The organisers did not keep the swap; your timeslot stays yours.
espace.aide.suivi.def.refuseeCible: The colleague did not want the swap; the request is closed.
espace.aide.suivi.alerte: A box saying “this swap would cause a problem” means the swap runs into a rule: rest time too short, that hour already taken, a stand expecting you at the same moment. It is a warning, not a refusal: the request is passed on anyway.
espace.aide.suivi.annulation: While a request is undecided, “Cancel this request” withdraws it. If the organisers added a comment to their decision, it shows just below.
espace.aide.recues.question: A colleague is asking me for a swap
espace.aide.recues.resume: They are waiting for your agreement: nothing moves until you answer.
espace.aide.recues.intro: Requests addressed to you show at the top of “My swaps”, under “Received requests”. Read the timeslot you are offered to take over and, if there is one, the timeslot taken from you in return.
espace.aide.recues.item1: “I agree” passes the request to the organisers, who decide: your agreement alone is not enough.
espace.aide.recues.item2: “Decline” closes the request, and your colleague is informed.
espace.aide.foire.question: Why can I not propose a swap?
espace.aide.foire.resume: The schedule fair is not open — not yet, or no longer.
espace.aide.foire.intro: The schedule fair is the period during which the organisers accept swaps. Once it is closed — the schedule is frozen, or the event has started — you keep access to your schedule and your past requests, but you can no longer propose, agree to or cancel one.
espace.aide.foire.suite: Something comes up after it closes? Tell the organisers directly: they can still act, this espace cannot.
espace.aide.contact.question: A mistake, a question?
espace.aide.contact.resume: The organisers stay your contact; this espace does not replace a phone call.
espace.aide.contact.item1: An assignment looks wrong, or an unavailability you announced was not taken into account: report it. Outside a collection period, you cannot correct your own data.
espace.aide.contact.item2: Last-minute impediment: tell them right away, without waiting for a swap request to be validated.
espace.aide.contact.item3: What the application knows about you and what it does with it is described in the privacy policy, in the menu at the top right.

aide.jourJ.title: Event-day mode
aide.jourJ.summary: Somebody has not shown up: mark them absent, find a replacement, apply — without starting a solve.
aide.jourJ.intro: Every other screen works ahead of the event. This one is meant for the day itself, standing in the aisle, on a phone: few taps, big targets, and three steps in the order of the gesture — who is missing, what places that opens, who can take them.
aide.jourJ.portee: Marking someone absent declares them unavailable on the remaining timeslots of the day, and on those only. A timeslot is remaining as long as it has not ended, the one in progress included. Past timeslots are never touched: the person really did hold them. The seat of a timeslot already started is not emptied either — the past no longer changes, the absence is merely recorded on it.
aide.jourJ.refus: An absence is applied entirely or not at all. It is refused, writing nothing, if it contradicts a forced assignment — the message names both adjustments — or if one of the seats to free is locked.
aide.jourJ.suggestions: For each place opened, the assistant offers the viable replacements, best first, and offers none that would break a hard rule. It stops at the first twenty eligible candidates and always shows how many it evaluated, so a shortened list is not read as “there is nobody else”. Applying a suggestion reassigns that one seat.
aide.jourJ.publication: Nothing is sent to the staff from this screen: their espace keeps showing the published schedule until you publish again. The banner says how many people are waiting for a change and points to the Publish button, on the Publication page.
aide.jourJ.trace: Every absence marked is a manual adjustment on record, with its reason, its author and its timestamp: you find it again the next day on the Adjustments tab of Instructions to the solver. It can be undone timeslot by timeslot or in one go, but the seats already reassigned do not come back on their own.
dateMock.tooltip: MOCK — today's date is frozen to {$date} on this server: the screens that reason about “now” are not showing reality. Click to change or clear that date.
jourJ.resume.vide: No timeslot is scheduled on that day: there is no journée to cover.
aide.jourJ.journee: The day starts at its first timeslot, not at midnight. An evening running past midnight therefore stays the same day, and at one in the morning the screen still shows yesterday's as long as its last timeslot runs. When nothing is running, the screen says so and invents no day.
jourJ.wip.message: Screen under development, and it acts: marking somebody absent writes real unavailabilities and empties real seats of the saved plan. Its effects are not guaranteed yet.
jourJ.wip.marche: marking somebody absent over the remaining timeslots of the day, undoing that absence, and applying a proposed replacement — each of those writes to the saved plan straight away
jourJ.wip.manque: any check of overall consistency without starting a solve, and handing the seats back when an absence is undone

aide.views.def.banc: The panel that opens on the right of the Planning page when a cell is clicked — a name or a free seat of the table, a shift of the rail, the “Seat” button of a stand on the map, “Open the seat” on a break nobody relieves, the seat icon in the changes. It gives the stand, the timeslot, who holds the seat and the locks freezing it; on a held seat, “Why them?” names the rules in default in the words of Planning rules, then come “Replace” (the viable replacements, searched on the saved planning under the edition's rules, with “Apply”), “Move to…”, “Free”, “Lock” or “Unlock”, “Who can hold this seat?” read-only, and “Open their profile”. “Free” asks for confirmation and, as long as “Keep them off this timeslot at the next solve” stays ticked, locks the person off that timeslot: without it, “Fix the rest” could put them straight back. “Apply” and “Free” only touch the seat if the person shown still holds it. On an empty seat, “Who can hold this seat?” opens the former bench, narrowed to that seat: who is on duty nowhere at that moment, and what would stop each of them holding it — every reason, not only the first. The people available come first, with “Place”; those a hard rule keeps out unfold on request. “Place” assigns the person and, as long as “Keep them at the next solve” stays ticked, locks them on that timeslot so the next solve leaves them there; the server refuses, naming the rule, a placement that would break a hard rule, and warns when it costs quality. “Place” is offered neither to a person a lock keeps off that timeslot — the line says so — nor on a timeslot already started. “Add an adjustment” opens the manual adjustment form, pre-filled with that stand and that timeslot. After a gesture, the panel says what is left to do: “Not published: Notify” leads to the publication, and “Fix the rest” starts an incremental solve when the gesture left a seat empty. Escape or the cross closes it. The palette finds the panel when you type “bench”.

aide.views.def.railJour: The same day seen per person: one line per staff member, the shifts placed in time. Gaps, daily spans and sequences jump out, and empty lines show who is still available — those marked “unavailable” say not to call on the person. A click on a shift opens its seat's panel; from the keyboard, Space on a line opens it on the line's shift — on the next one, pressed again — and Enter opens “Move a shift of …”, whether drag and drop is on or not. When it is, a shift can also be dragged onto another line, under the same conditions as on the table of the day.
aide.views.def.kpi: One row per finished solve, all editions together: score, coverage, spread of hours, number of manual changes, duration, and the dosage the solve was launched under — « default », « N rule(s) reweighted », or « unknown » for a row older than this measure, with the detail on hover. A row's filter button keeps only the solves computed under the same dosage, to compare at equal weights. Above the table, the replay walks one edition's solves — the current edition by default, a deleted edition can still be chosen: one small curve per measure, each on its own scale, a cursor moved with the mouse, the arrow keys or the buttons, and a playback that advances one solve per second (five past a hundred), disabled when the browser asks to limit animations. The card says what moved since the previous solve, rules that appeared or disappeared included, and a band shows the coverage day by day — « not measured » for a solve older than this measure. The table follows the chosen edition and highlights the pointed solve; a click on a row puts the cursor there. A row deleted by hand drops out of the replay without leaving a gap: the ranks close up. It is the memory of past campaigns. Nothing in it names anyone, and the history survives the deletion of the edition it describes.

aide.views.def.carteJour: The same day on the map of locations: a time cursor, and each location coloured by what is happening there at that instant — open and fully filled, open with empty places, or open with nobody. Stands with no geolocated location are listed next to the map. Each pin carries the number of people present, followed by the seats planned, and grows with the headcount; hovering details the split by stand. Below the map, the « Load per location » grid crosses each location with the spans of the day — a span starts or ends as soon as a seat opens or closes — and gives in each cell present / seats, the last row being the total on site; stands with no location have their own row. A click or Enter on a cell puts the cursor on that span. « Whole event » switches to one column per day, each cell giving the peak of the day. A person on a relayed break stays counted on their stand; an empty seat, or one freed by a day-of absence, counts nobody.
aide.views.def.comparaisonJours: On the table and the rail of the Planning page, “Compare with…” puts a second day next to the first — two Saturdays, for instance. A banner gives, for each day, the seats to fill, filled and empty, the breaks without relief, the staff on duty and the stands open, with the difference of the second day over the first. Below, one line per stand (or per staff member on the rail), in the same order on both sides: a stand closed on one of the two days is greyed there, and the lines that differ — hours, seats or number of seats filled — carry the word “difference”. “Differences only” hides the rest, the page's filters apply to both days — the banner then counts the lines kept only and says “filtered” —, and two shortcuts offer the same day the previous or next week. The comparison is read-only: drag and drop comes back when you leave it. The review panel is hidden, since a review covers one whole day; each column only says whether its day is reviewed. On a phone, the two days are read through tabs A and B. The address keeps both days: reloading or sharing it reopens the same comparison.

espace.aide.dispo.intro: Before building the schedule, the organisers open a period during which everyone says which days they cannot come, and which kinds of games they would like to run. The days of the event show as chips: tap the ones that do not work.
espace.aide.dispo.etape1: Tap every day you cannot come. Days you do not tap mean “I am available”.
espace.aide.dispo.etape2: Pick the kinds of games you would enjoy. A wish is not a guarantee: it is honoured when the schedule allows it.
espace.aide.dispo.etape3: Add a word if your situation does not fit in boxes (“I am leaving on Sunday after lunch”).
espace.aide.dispo.etape4: Send. The form already opens on what the organisation knows about you: you correct, you do not start from scratch.
espace.aide.dispo.item1: What you send is a proposal: nothing is recorded on your file until the organisers apply it.
espace.aide.dispo.item2: You can send a corrected version while the collection is open: it replaces the previous one.
espace.aide.dispo.item3: Your skills are not declared here: they stay decided with the organisation.
espace.aide.dispo.item4: Once the collection is closed, the tab stays readable but accepts nothing more. Tell the organisers directly instead.
espace.aide.dispo.avant: If the collection has not started yet, the tab gives the date to come back on. It is not a refusal: there is nothing to do until then.
espace.aide.dispo.attente: Once sent, your declaration shows at the top of the tab under “Your pending declaration”, with its date. While it says that, the organisers have not dealt with it, and sending again replaces it.
espace.aide.dispo.historique: Further down, “My previous declarations” keeps a trace of what you sent and what became of it: “Taken into account”, “Not retained” or “Waiting for the organisation”, with the note attached to the decision if there is one. “Not retained” does not mean lost: correct it and send again while the collection is open.
espace.aide.foire.avant: Two situations look alike on screen. If the fair is not open yet, the tab gives the date to come back on: nothing to do until then. If it is closed, every request goes through the organisers.

aide.dispo.title: Availability and preference collection
aide.dispo.summary: Staff declare their own absences and wishes; you apply them, or not.
aide.dispo.intro: Before building a schedule, you need to know who cannot come when. Rather than collecting that outside the application and retyping it, open a collection window: everyone declares from their espace, on their phone, their unavailable days and the games they would like to run. What they send touches nothing: it is a proposal, waiting for your decision.
aide.dispo.def.fenetre: The collection opens and closes on the Settings page, Edition tab, Counters card; the Availability page keeps a one-line state of it, with a button to close it. Carpooling follows it: it opens and closes with it. Unlike the schedule fair, the collection is closed until you open it. Both dates are optional and bound the period; the switch stays in charge. Closed, the espace refuses any declaration server-side, but the person keeps access to what they declared and to your answers.
aide.dispo.def.prevenir: A checkbox at opening time, never a permanent setting: it sends everyone the link to their espace, straight to the declaration tab. Tick it on the first round; leave it alone when you reopen after a fix, otherwise everybody gets a chaser for nothing.
aide.dispo.term.decision: Apply or refuse, as a whole
aide.dispo.def.decision: The screen shows side by side what the person declares and what their record says today. Applying writes the whole proposal onto their record; the saved schedule is then flagged as stale, and regenerating stays a separate action. Refusing changes nothing, and your reason is read by the person in their espace. There is deliberately no line-by-line approval: a disagreement is settled with a word, and the person sends a corrected version.
aide.dispo.def.remplacement: Someone who corrects themselves replaces their pending proposal, they do not stack a second one: you will never have two contradictory versions to arbitrate. You are only notified when a proposal arrives, not on every correction they make before you deal with it.
aide.dispo.def.competences: Skills stay decided with you: a self-declared skill feeds hard rules — who may hold which stand — where an unavailability or a wish can be made up for. Someone declaring a day outside the event dates, or a category that does not exist, is refused on submission.

aide.shortcuts.tables: The reference-data tables can also be browsed from the keyboard. The shortest route: “/” puts the cursor in the filter, type enough to narrow the list, then Down jumps onto the first row.
aide.shortcuts.def.rowEnter: Enters the table without counting tab stops: focus jumps onto the current row. Clicking a row focuses it the same way.

aide.importGrille.title: Stand grid import
aide.importGrille.summary: Pour in the spreadsheet matrix — stands in rows, days and timeslots in columns — without retyping it.
aide.importGrille.format: The tab reads a CSV as a spreadsheet exports it: a first column naming the stand by its code, or failing that by its exact name, then one column per day and per timeslot, one headcount per cell, empty, “-” or 0 for closed. Two header rows — the dates, then the bands “10h00-12h00” — or a single one, “2026-07-08 10h00-12h00”. The simplest is to start from “Download the current grid as a template”.
aide.importGrille.colonnes: Each column lands on the timeslot of the same date that contains its hours; a narrower column writes a window at its own bounds. A column with no timeslot is ignored and listed, without the file being refused. A timeslot the file does not name keeps the current cell of each imported stand. With no timeslot at all in the edition, the import is refused.
aide.importGrille.stands: An accepted stand is rewritten as from the entry grid: its whole schedule follows its cells, and its minimum and maximum headcounts follow the smallest and the largest.
