aide.views.def.marge: The day crossed with the time band, and in each cell the staff available minus the seats to fill. Red below zero, green above. “Before solving” compares raw capacity with the seats to fill and therefore answers with no computation at all; “after solving” only counts as free those not already on a seat and not ruled out by a hard rule, against the seats left empty. The reading is optimistic: a negative cell really is negative, a comfortable cell guarantees nothing.
aide.views.def.tension: Third reading of the Margin, once a schedule is persisted: the margin after the solve crossed with the fragility. Critical: empty seats nobody can hold, a seat nobody else could take over, or a stand with no specialist — the cell is then hatched. High: a zero margin with empty seats, or more fragile seats (one substitute at most) than people to spare. Watched: fragile seats but enough margin, or a single-specialist stand with no polyvalent as backup. Calm otherwise. The « 2 ⚠ » badge counts the fragile seats; a cell opens its reasons, with “Who can hold an empty seat” — the seat panel, on the Planning page —, the fiche of the irreplaceable person and the fragility of the stand. A timeslot already started is greyed out.

aide.relecture.title: Reviewing the planning before publishing
aide.relecture.summary: Mark where you are in your review, day by day — without freezing anything.
aide.relecture.intro: Between the first schedule that holds and the mailing to the staff there is a review: you open the days one by one, look, fix. Over twelve days, the real question is “where had I got to?”. On the Planning page, the review bar's menu opens “Reviewed and accepted…”, whose “Mark reviewed and accepted” records your pass, with the date and a comment if you leave one. The day selector then marks the reviewed days, and the Solver page says “3 days out of 12”.
aide.relecture.journeeEntiere: Acceptance always covers the whole day. The page filters change what you are looking at, not what you accept. To review stand by stand, filter, go through, then accept the day once the round is done.
aide.relecture.verrou: Accepting a day does not freeze it. A planning lock stops the solver touching seats; an acceptance says a human has reviewed, and lets the computation improve the rest. The “Also lock this day” box sits next to it because the two gestures often go together, never because one would imply the other.
aide.relecture.prerequis: The review bar, under the day selector, counts what to look at: empty seats, breaks without relay, locked seats, changes since the publication. A click on a chip narrows the rendering to what it counts — the table to its empty or locked seats, the breaks to those without relay, the changes — and a second click gives it back whole. Before you accept, “Reviewed and accepted…” also shows the hard gaps and the seats resting on someone irreplaceable: the figures of the Problems, Breaks and Fragility screens, filtered on the date. None of them blocks: if you know why a seat stays empty, accept and write it in the comment.
aide.relecture.resolution: A solve that moves a seat on a day you had accepted removes that acceptance, and the summary says so: nobody has reviewed what the computation has just written. A day that was also locked keeps its acceptance, since nothing could move there. When publishing, the panel reminds you how many unreviewed days would go out.
aide.relecture.changements: The « Changes » rendering of the Planning page lists what moved on that day: seat by seat (stand, timeslot, who was there, who is now) or person by person, in the very sentences of the publication mail. Two references: since the last publication — what people were sent — or since the last solve, to see what the solver just rewrote. The last solve is the one that actually replaced the saved schedule: an interrupted or refused solve does not move that mark, and a restore or an import made between two solves count among the changes. Somebody kept on their stand with trimmed hours reads as « hours changed », not removed then new. The counters follow the page's filters and say so. As long as no reference exists, the tab says so rather than counting zero changes.
aide.start.avertissements: An entry that is questionable but workable is saved with a warning to read, never refused in silence. A refusal, on the other hand, shows in red and writes nothing.
aide.editions.intro: An edition is an event — or a plan variant — with its own stands, staff, timeslots, settings and schedule. Nothing travels from one edition to another: “2025” stays readable while “2026” is being prepared. The edition you are looking at is per browser tab, and the top banner says which one.
aide.data.suppression: Before a deletion, the confirmation states what references the selection — assignments, manual adjustments, planning locks. That is information, not a lock: no figure prevents deletion.
aide.creneaux.title: Timeslots and day templates
aide.creneaux.summary: The time grid the solver fills, and how to write it without typing it day by day.
aide.creneaux.intro: A timeslot is a day, a date and two times. It is the grid the solver fills: on each timeslot, every open stand gets as many seats as its opening window names. Timeslots are shared by every stand — you never create one per stand, it is the opening hours that say what each one opens. And the dates of the timeslots are the dates of the edition.
aide.creneaux.grille: A grid of timeslots is always made of shifts: real stretches of work. The page states what the grid holds — opening spans still to be split, or final shifts — because every verdict depends on it: an overlap is an error between opening spans, and the normal form of staggered shifts. The “Grid check” runs by itself, on every visit and after every write, and shows as a banner under the calendar, its details to unfold. Every timeslot of the list counts its “Open stands · seats”, a link to the stand hours on that day.
aide.creneaux.def.journeesTypes: Describe each kind of day once — “Ordinary day”, “Late night”, “Set-up” — by its vacations on one line: “09:00-12:00, 12:00-13:00 R, 13:00-14:00 R, 14:00-20:00”, an R marking a meal relay where the stand only holds half its seats. A calendar then puts a day template on each date.
aide.creneaux.def.appliquer: Writes the timeslots, after a numbered preview. An identical timeslot keeps its seats, a surplus timeslot on a governed date is removed, a date with no day template is left alone. A day template edited afterwards changes nothing until you apply again: its dates move to “out of step”.
aide.creneaux.def.serie: The same thing without memory, for a one-off need: in a day template's dialog, this button lays its timeslots on the chosen days, after a preview, without keeping the day template. The meal relays do not follow.
aide.creneaux.term.deriver: Derive from the stands' opening hours
aide.creneaux.def.deriver: When the stands already have their opening hours, the grid can follow from them: a cut at every opening or closing time, a timeslot on every stretch where at least one stand is open. Previewed, then added to the grid; “Replace the grid…” puts it in place of the current one, after a confirmation saying the computed plan goes with it. Along with recognition, it sits in the “Other ways to build the grid” menu, next to adding a single timeslot.
aide.creneaux.term.reconnaitre: Recognise day templates from the time slots
aide.creneaux.def.reconnaitre: The other way round, on a grid already written: the application infers the day templates and the calendar that carries them.
aide.creneaux.enchainement: Two timeslots that touch do chain for the same person: nothing requires a gap between two vacations. What decides is how long the stretch they form is — past six hours it owes a break, taken as a gap or relayed by a colleague of the stand.
aide.ouvertures.title: Stand hours
aide.ouvertures.summary: Enter each stand's headcount on each slot, as in a spreadsheet, and see straight away what the solver will read.
aide.ouvertures.intro: Open this screen before any solve. Entering and checking happen in one place: each cell says what the solver will read once the rules are expanded and the exceptions and the day's consigne applied. The summary and the anomalies sit above the grid: a stand open on no day at all, a window outside the hours of the day, a stretch too short to be a shift. Each anomaly leads to the stand's form, or to the slot grid when that is what is at fault.
aide.ouvertures.def.parJourneeType: Available as soon as the edition has day templates: one column per vacation, one cell standing at once for every date that template governs. Sixty columns become about fifteen. A cell showing “≠” flags dates that do not say the same thing; retyping it aligns them. While they diverge it says nothing to spread: applying its column is refused rather than deciding for you.
aide.ouvertures.def.comparer: Two to eight stands laid on the same days and the same columns, for instance the bars that should share the same opening hours. They are picked one by one or by game category; the first one is the reference, and another can take that role. Each cell that departs from the reference is framed and says the kind of difference — opening, hours or headcount. The comparison is about what the solver will read: a rule and dated exceptions that open the same way make no difference. The summary counts, per stand, the days that differ and gives the first one; « Only the days that differ » hides the others. Below the grid, each stand's rules and exceptions side by side, a rule absent from the reference or missing being flagged. A day under a consigne is marked. The comparator writes nothing: « Copy the reference's opening hours to… » opens the stands' bulk edit, set to « Replace with another stand's », which waits for its own save. It is also reached from the Stands page, through the selection or through « Compare with… » in a stand's record; the address keeps the selection.
aide.ouvertures.enregistrement: On save, every stand you changed has its whole schedule rewritten from its cells, folded back into rules when a pattern repeats; its minimum and maximum headcounts follow the smallest and largest cell. A dotted cell carries a bound no column follows: saved as is it keeps its windows, retyped it applies to the whole column. “Align partial windows” extends them all, saying first how many hours that adds.
aide.ouvertures.fermetures: A stand does not have to declare its closures: any day not declared is closed. “Compact the schedules”, in the “More” menu of the Stands page, removes the closures that have become pointless, after checking that no opening moves.
aide.ouvertures.chevauchements: Three more points are reported for information, never blocking a save: two rules of one stand that overlap (the higher headcount then counts), a rule no day applies because a more precise rule or a dated exception replaces it everywhere, two windows of one rule that overlap at different headcounts. The rule editor of the stand form says them live under the rule concerned, and shows when a more precise rule takes precedence over another, for instance a weekend closure over an every-day opening.
aide.competences.enregistrer: Nothing is written before “Save”: changed cells are outlined, the button counts the records concerned, and leaving the page unsaved asks for confirmation. The heart of a cell says the person wishes for that category: a click, or the S key, sets or removes it, and it is saved with the rest — the level is entered alongside the wish, without either deciding the other. While a solve runs, entry is locked.
aide.importCsv.onglet.typologies: Categories, locations, stands: a code and a label are enough — the code is the key other files quote; a row without a code is designated by its label or name, and an identifier is never read, the application assigns it. Latitude and longitude are optional for a location; the headcount is optional for a stand, which then holds with one person. A category a stand names without it existing is created, and the preview names it.
aide.importCsv.onglet.creneaux: Timeslots and day templates: a timeslot is recognised by its date and its two times, so replaying a file updates the grid instead of doubling it. A day template is recognised by its name. Careful: importing day templates moves no timeslot — the grid only moves when you apply the calendar.
aide.importCsv.onglet.animateurs: Staff: the most useful one, detailed below.
aide.importCsv.onglet.grille: Stand grid: the spreadsheet matrix, stands in rows, days and timeslots in columns. It has its own section in this guide.
aide.importCsv.onglet.scenario: Scenario: a YAML file that carries the whole edition and replaces it instead of adding to it.
aide.importCsv.etape1: Save the sheet as “CSV UTF-8”. The .xlsx is not read, and another encoding is refused — its accents are already lost.
aide.importCsv.etape2: Drop the file and say which column is which field. A mapping is proposed from the headers, you correct it.
aide.importCsv.etape3: Read the preview: every row is announced accepted or rejected, with its line number and the reason.
aide.importCsv.etape4: Validate. By default the import adds and updates without deleting anyone, and unavailable days add to those already recorded. Two checkboxes reverse each of those choices.
aide.importCsv.callout.title: The two refusals that surprise you
aide.importCsv.callout.text: Create your timeslots first: with no event dates, an imported unavailable day would be invisible in the espace, then erased. And give every new record a date of birth: the whole minor / adult bracket depends on it. A row designates a record by its e-mail address, failing that by its first and last name — never by an identifier. If two people share a name, add an e-mail column: the import refuses the row rather than choosing for you.
aide.importCsv.remplacement: If you tick full replacement, read the warning in the preview: deleting a record also takes away that person's availability declaration, their acknowledgement and their espace access code.
aide.importGrille.heures: The template writes its bands with an “h” on purpose: Excel turns “13:00-16:00” into a date, and the band is then lost.
aide.calculer.attente: When the solver is busy, each of the three buttons schedules the computation instead of refusing it: it will start by itself as soon as the running task finishes.
aide.calculer.bloquants: When the feasibility banner carries a problem no run can solve — two manual adjustments that contradict each other, a forced assignment nobody can honour — the three buttons ask for confirmation before starting, and name the cause: the run would end on a negative hard score however long it runs. Solving anyway stays possible, the rest of the schedule still improves. A shortage of staff asks nothing: the solver still fills what it can.
aide.results.callout.title: Points that measure nothing
aide.results.callout.text: A constraint that penalises every seat for want of data entered — no wish declared, no referent — produces a constant floor, sometimes most of the total. On the Planning rules page, a rule penalising at least 95 % of what it evaluates carries a mark in its Violations column; its panel names the missing data and points to the screen where to enter it. Nothing is switched off for you. Compare scores between two solves of the same data, never their absolute value.
aide.jourJ.callout.title: This screen really acts
aide.jourJ.callout.text: It is still under development, and it differs from the other trial screens on one point: marking someone absent writes real unavailabilities and empties real seats from the saved schedule, right away. No solve re-checks the whole thing meanwhile. Run one as soon as the situation allows.
aide.views.intro: All these views read the saved schedule; none of them starts a computation. As long as no solve has run, they say so instead of staying empty.
aide.foire.echange: There they see their up-to-date schedule and can propose swapping a timeslot with a colleague, either simply giving it up or also naming the timeslot they want in return. The colleague agrees first, from their own espace: a request only reaches your Swaps screen once both agree, and a refusal closes it with no arbitration. Every request is pre-checked against the hard rules; an unworkable one is flagged, but passed on anyway — you are the one who decides.
aide.foire.notifications: If mail is configured, you are notified by e-mail on every submission. The staff member, for their part, learns the fate of their requests at the next publication: approving a swap changes the working plan, not yet the one they received.

aide.consignes.title: Consignes (order, heatwave)
aide.consignes.summary: Close every stand on a time band of a few days, by decision, and reopen on compensation windows — destroying nothing.
aide.consignes.intro: A prefectural order lands the evening before: from noon to 6 pm nobody outside, for three days of an event that lasts ten. Then it is extended, then lifted. The Consignes tab of the Instructions to the solver page holds that gesture as one line per date: the closed band, the motif — required, it is printed wherever the day is shown as modified — and the stands reopened in compensation, in the evening or the morning.
aide.consignes.etape.poser: Lay down: pick a preset (« Heatwave plan »: band, motif, default windows) or type freely, then the dates. Only the grid's days to come are offered: a day already begun keeps for good the consigne that governed it.
aide.consignes.etape.stands: The stands are read for the first date and the band: those losing minutes arrive ticked, with the default windows and the inherited headcount — the highest headcount lost in the band. A stand that typed dated hours that day is set aside, with the reason, but stays tickable. Each window carries its own headcount — empty, it inherits; a stand may reopen at 2 in the morning and at 7 in the evening. Filter by name, category, location or premium; « Apply to the selection » sets the windows, or the headcount of every window, of the displayed ticked stands in one go.
aide.consignes.etape.apercu: « Preview » says, date by date, what the write would do: seats and minutes before and after, time slots to add or remove, shifts without a seat, stands entering and leaving, minors concerned, locks and adjustments touched, staff seated in the band, and whether the review acceptance will be withdrawn. « Save » sends exactly the same request.
aide.consignes.etape.modifier: Modify replaces a date's consigne in place, Extend carries its band, motif and openings onto other dates, Lift removes it from the chosen dates — the time slots it had added leave with their seats. All three gestures are previewed, and refused on a date already begun.
aide.consignes.etape.resolution: The plan then follows the ordinary path: an incremental solve puts people back on the time slots that remain and on those added, then the publication announces the days with modified hours. The staff space, the event-day screen and the individual PDF print the motif under the date — for the person whose whole day the band emptied too, who reads « Repos » and the reason.
aide.consignes.callout.title: Nothing is destroyed
aide.consignes.term.relancer: Re-solving after a consigne: lock, then run a full solve
aide.consignes.def.relancer: Put a « day » lock on every day to keep, then run a full solve: it restarts from the plan in place and only touches the free days. Avoid the incremental re-solve here — it pins every seat whose holder is still available, including, after a lift, an afternoon grown back to 2 pm-8 pm next to another seat, and it trades seats far too slowly when a saturated evening leaves one empty.
aide.consignes.term.soirBloque: The evening stays half empty: the meal break
aide.consignes.def.soirBloque: An evening window behind a shortened afternoon — 6 pm-10 pm behind a 2 pm-8 pm cut to 6 pm-8 pm — needs two people per seat as long as the evening meal break (7 pm-9 pm) forbids chaining 6 pm-8 pm then 8 pm-10 pm. The answer is in the consigne itself, section “Meal windows on that day”: align the evening window on the compensation (6 pm-10 pm) and give the reason — the teams ate during the closure. It holds on those dates only and leaves with the consigne; the edition's parameters never move. Then solve again. The other lever is reopening fewer stands in the evening. The eleven-hour daily rest is not at stake.
aide.consignes.callout.text: The band closes every stand, without exception, above their rules and their dated exceptions — and it closes only that: an unticked stand keeps its hours outside the band. Nominal time slots keep their id, their seats and their locks; the band's shifts simply become seatless. The time slots missing to cover a window are added and marked « added by consigne »; day templates ignore those dates, shown « under consigne » rather than drifted. Statistics count the hours actually worked, and a snapshot carries the consignes in force at its capture.

aide.tuning.playbook: Under each problem of the Diagnostic, the « What to do? » block offers the gestures that solve it, most likely first, each with a sentence of explanation and a button opening the screen already positioned. No button writes anything: the screen it opens keeps its own previews and confirmations, and you decide. For an understaffed timeslot: see who could come (the seat panel, on the Planning page at that timeslot's day, where “Place” fills the place), then add a skill on the stand's game category, then lower the staffing asked, finally review the days off of that day. For a legal rule in default: propose a repair from the Planning page, or look for a replacement from the seat panel — a legal rule is not a setting. For a quality rule: lower its importance, the Planning rules page opens on its panel. For a floor rule: enter the missing data first. For a break nobody can relieve: open a relief seat on the stand, or shorten the shift. For manual adjustments or a lock involved: review them, shown on their own. A day already started offers nothing that would change it: its plan is frozen as worked. The explanation of a rule repeats the advice of its panel in Planning rules word for word.

aide.views.def.fiche: Everything known about one person on one page, and everything done for them from that page. At the top, the gestures: “Copy the espace link”, “Send their planning” (the same e-mail as the publication, for them alone, after a confirmation), “Remind”, the PDF and the ICS of their planning, “Lock their whole planning” or “Release their whole planning”, “Add an adjustment” (the form, already in their name) and “Edit the profile”. Previous and next walk the list of the Animateurs page as you filtered and sorted it. Seven foldable sections, the first three open: identity and contact; availability, on a strip of the days — click a day, then “Unavailable that day”: the day is written among their unavailable days and, if the persisted plan seats them that day, their seats of that day are freed in the same gesture (a seat already started stays as it is; so does a locked seat, which the fiche names with the “Manage locks” link); each freed seat offers “Who can hold this seat?”, and “Cancel the absence” makes the day available again without handing the seats back; the planning, day by day — opening span, shifts, meal breaks, pauses and walks —, each shift leading to the Planning page with its seat open; load and fairness, their line of “By person” with the gap to the median and the radar, “Compare with…” laying a second person on it; competences and wishes, editable in place; fragility, with “Lock” and “Train” on each fragile seat; swaps and follow-up — publication, acknowledgement, requests, adjustments, locks. The figures are those of the specialised screens, never recomputed. Every animateur name in the application leads here.

aide.adHoc.def.arriveeGroupee: 2 to 4 people who arrive and leave together. A preference, not a hard rule: the solver tries to give them the same days, and first arrivals and last departures within the tolerance — the “Grouped arrival tolerance” setting, 30 min by default, on the rule's row in Planning rules, Quality tab; beyond it, every minute of gap and every day a member works without the others costs. Each may work a different stand. No timeslot, no stand. It usually comes from an “I'm coming with…” request sent from the Carpool tab of the espace and validated on the Availabilities page, Carpool tab; it can also be created by hand here. One that comes from a validated request can neither be edited nor deleted here: its buttons are greyed out and lead to Availability, Carpool tab, where cancelling it notifies the group; one written by hand stays editable. It is refused when two of its members form an incompatibility with neither stand nor timeslot: you do not have two people arrive together whom you refuse to have work together.

The request is sent and decided apart from the declaration — applying or refusing a declaration never touches it. It lands on the “Carpool” tab of this page (the number waiting shows on the tab), one card per request: “Confirmed by all” when every member named exactly the same group, and the number of days on which their declared unavailabilities differ — on those days, they cannot arrive together.

aide.dispo.def.covoiturageDecision: Each request is decided on its own. “Validate the grouped arrival” creates a “Grouped arrival” manual adjustment naming the requester and their teammates; the other members' requests naming the same group are validated with it, and an identical group already present is joined rather than doubled. The planning only takes it into account at the next solve. “Set aside” writes nothing: an optional reason (500 characters at most) is read by the animateur in their espace, and they may send a new request while the collection is open. Either way, the people concerned receive an e-mail — each member for a validation, the requester for a setting aside; a send that fails does not undo the decision. Once validated, the group can no longer be changed from the espace, nor from the Adjustments tab of Instructions to the solver: it is cancelled from here.

aide.mural.summary: A screen for the control room TV: who holds which stand now and next, updated every minute, with no admin session.
aide.mural.intro: Settings, “Wall display” tab: give the link a label (“Security desk TV”), pick the locations to show if needed — one TV per zone — and create it. The address is shown only once: copy it or scan the QR code with the device driving the TV. Once lost it cannot be recovered: create another link and revoke the old one.
aide.mural.ecran: The screen groups the stands open today by location. Each tile shows the shift under way and the next one, with the names and, in red, every empty seat; a stand closed at that moment is dimmed with its reopening time. At the bottom: seats to fill within two hours, breaks without relay and the day's consigne. When everything does not fit, the pages turn every fifteen seconds.
aide.mural.donnees: What is shown is the saved schedule, not the one sent to the animateurs: a replacement made in Event-day mode shows up within a minute, without republishing. The time is the server's, never the TV's. If the network drops, the screen keeps what it showed and says since when it has been offline.
aide.mural.noms: By default the screen shows the first name and the initial of the last name: everyone in the room can see it. Full names are an option of the link, chosen when it is created. No phone number, age or reason for absence ever appears on it.
aide.mural.securite: The link opens this screen only, for this edition, read-only. The list of links gives the date of the last read; revoking a link cuts the screen at its next read, and deleting the edition takes its links along. For a large-format poster of the whole day, add ?impression=1 to the address and print the page — or, with no link, “Print this day” on the Planning page, behind your session.

aide.start.step2.fichiers: Enter the reference data in the order of the Prepare group: categories, time slots (this is where the edition gets its dates), locations, stands, staff. Each one can also be imported from a CSV file or a spreadsheet paste, through the “Import” button of its screen or through the Files page; a YAML scenario replaces the whole step.
aide.start.demo: To discover the application without entering anything, load an example: Files page, Import tab, “Examples” card. “Festival réaliste — canicule” is a real, anonymised sixteen-day edition; it arrives in an edition of its own name, without touching yours.
aide.jourJ.mock.instance: This screen only talks about today, which makes it hard to explore outside the event period. In development, or on a demonstration or staging server that allows it, the “Simulated date and time” card of Settings, Instance tab, freezes the date and time the server takes as now; an hourglass then appears in the top bar and leads back to the field, and “Back to the machine's clock” lifts it. The espace follows the same clock. On a production instance, the setting does not exist.
aide.shortcuts.disable.instance: If you dictate by voice, or a key slips, turn the single-key shortcuts off: a checkbox in the list of shortcuts (“?”) and in Settings, Instance tab. The setting holds for this browser; Ctrl+K, the menu and the addresses remain.
aide.editions.vider: “Empty this edition”, at the bottom of the Editions page, deletes the stands, time slots, staff, assignments, manual adjustments, locks, day validations, swap requests, consignes and consigne presets of the edition you are viewing, once its name has been typed back. Its categories, locations, day templates, snapshots and settings remain, as do the other editions and the instance settings. Refused during a solve and while a family is frozen.
aide.importCsv.ecran.fichiers: Every file that fills an edition is on the “Files” screen, Import tab, one card per reference table, in the order the data holds together; the “Import” button of each reference screen opens the same card without leaving the screen, and each card also accepts a paste from a spreadsheet. Nothing is written until you have validated the preview, and a column the file does not carry erases nothing: renaming stands with a three-column file touches neither their opening hours nor their location.
aide.importCsv.exports.fichiers: The Export tab of the same page goes the other way: a ZIP archive, one file per reference table, in the exact shape these cards read back. That is what lets you copy one edition onto another, or fix things in bulk in a spreadsheet and import again.
aide.calculer.def.passe.instance: While the event is under way, all three computations take the seats of timeslots already started — a past day, or a timeslot of today whose hour has come — from the saved schedule and freeze them as they were worked, even if the person has since declared the day unavailable, even if the seat stayed empty. Those seats count towards rest, totals and days in a row, but no rule holds them against the plan: zero hard is read on what is still to play. The recap announces them (“seats already started”). In development, demonstration or staging, the date this rule reads is set from Settings, Instance tab; in operation, the PASSE_FIGE=false variable switches it off, to replay a past edition.
aide.exchange.item.fichiers: The Files page gathers the two halves of one gesture — export, correct in the spreadsheet, import again — and the archive that closes an edition, in three tabs: Import, Export, Archive. Each reference screen also has its own “Import” button, which opens the same card without leaving the screen.
aide.exchange.item.scenario.fichiers: Importing a YAML scenario (Files, Import tab, Scenario card): the fastest way to fill an empty edition. An invalid file gives a detailed notification rather than a partial import.
aide.exchange.item.exemples: Examples (Files, Import tab): the schedules shipped with the application, sorted “to discover”, “to test a case” and “extremes”, each with its size and what it shows.
aide.exchange.item.collage: Paste from a spreadsheet: each reference import card also accepts copied cells, headers included, and reads them like a file; the preview comes before any write. After an import, “See the … imported rows” opens the reference screen on those rows alone; “Show all” brings the whole list back there.
aide.exchange.item.exports.fichiers: Exports (Files, Export tab): the edition's reference data as a ZIP archive, or the whole edition as a scenario — in the exact shape the Import tab reads back.
aide.exchange.item.archive.fichiers: End-of-event archive (Files, Archive tab): a finished edition's exports in a single ZIP — overall planning, fairness, hours, reference data, scenario, review, individual schedules as you choose — with a LISEZMOI.txt manifest saying which plan they come from. No access token is in it, but names, birth dates and addresses are: once downloaded, keeping it is up to you. The edition status offers it once the last day is past.
aide.exchange.item.yamlValidator.fichier: Check a file without importing it (Files, Import tab): checks the structure of a scenario file without writing anything.
aide.exchange.item.debug.brut: Debug: the raw state returned by the server, the version, the API documentation and the technical checks — notification, error, test e-mail, Mailpit. Useful to report a problem precisely. It is not in the menu: Ctrl+K then “debug”, or its address /debug.
aide.exchange.item.sauvegarde.instance: Nightly backup (Settings page, Instance tab): the whole database is copied onto the server disk every night, and the screen says where, which copies exist and whether the last one went well. It cannot be downloaded — it carries everyone's names, dates of birth and addresses — and restoring is an operator task.

aide.rappels.def.rappel.accueil: The evening before, every staff member assigned the next day receives the list of their time slots. It is taken from the published schedule, never from the working plan: nobody is reminded of a slot you have not told them about. A staff member without an address is skipped: “To handle today” counts them while their day is ahead, and “Recent messages” names them.
aide.rappels.def.echanges.accueil: A request that has waited for your decision longer than the set delay turns into an alert in “To handle today”, on the home page. Its age counts from the colleague's agreement: a request still waiting for their answer is not waiting for you.
aide.start.accueil.phases: The home page takes the shape of the moment. While preparing, it goes through these steps as a checklist: each line says where you stand, with the figure that matters and a link to the screen that moves it forward; the last solve is read there in sentences, and the freeze of the reference data is recalled with the link to the Settings, the one place it is set. From the first to the last day of the event, the first line is the day's — “Today — D5 · stands open · empty seats · absent · swaps to decide” — and opens the event-day mode; “Show on the TV” leads to the wall display, and the checklist unfolds on demand. Once the event is over, the archive comes first. On an empty edition, a “Get started” block offers to import a file, to start from an edition or to load an example.
aide.start.aTraiter.accueil: At the top of the page, the “To handle today” box lists what waits for a decision: availability declarations to apply, swap requests to decide — flagged beyond the age set in the notification settings —, days not yet reviewed in the coming week, people silent since the publication and never reminded, data changed since the last solve, people to notify, and what could not leave, while its cause stands: a day-before reminder to a record still without an address, a reminder — nightly or by hand — to someone still silent, a failed nightly backup. Each line opens its screen with the filter already applied. Below it, “Recent messages” unfolds the alerts from the nightly sends, by name, and the history of the application's messages, to mark as read or to clear; the bell in the top bar leads to this box. “Today” is the server's, the simulated date when one is set.
aide.start.coherence.fusion: A closed warning is not lost: the “Referential coherence” line of the home page replays every check over everything entered — staff, time slots, stands and openings, manual adjustments, staffing need. It counts the anomalies; “Show the detail” unfolds them, identical anomalies making a single line with their count, “16 days: nothing between 12:00 and 13:00”, one line per subject with its severity and the link to the record that fixes it. A time slot that fell outside the openings because a stand changed afterwards shows up there, although no message flagged it when the stand was saved.
aide.gel.intro.parametres: Once the stands are ready, or the time slots settled, they are frozen: no path changes them any more — form, bulk edit, file import, assistant — until the freeze is lifted. The freeze is set family by family, in the current edition, from the Edition tab of the Settings — the edition status recalls it and leads there. The application offers it after the first computation and after the first publication, never imposes it.

aide.ouvertures.def.grille: One row per stand, one column per tranche of need, the headcount in each cell. Columns follow changes of headcount, not shifts — a stand whose headcount changes at 7 pm cuts the 14-20 slot into two columns for everybody. An empty cell is closed: empty it, or type “-” or 0, to close. A figure in italics was not entered: the stand, with no hours declared, follows its rule and opens by default. The moves of a spreadsheet — arrows, Enter, pasting a block, copying a day onto the other displayed days, taking the row above, applying a cell to its whole column. Those last two each have a button, shown on hover at the head of the row and of the column, and a shortcut: Ctrl+D and Ctrl+Shift+Down. A stand's name leads to its form; “From” and “To” narrow the grid to a few days.
aide.ouvertures.def.couches: Behind the figure, thin bars: at the bottom the opening kept, solid for a recurring rule, red for a dated exception; at the top the stand's hours before the consigne; over the whole height, tinted, the band the day's consigne closes; dotted, a slot the consigne added. “Show in the cells” hides each of these layers, and the address keeps the choice. A modified cell shows straight away the opening it will write. Clicking a cell explains it in one sentence above the grid, for instance “Open 14:00–18:00: recurring rule 14:00–20:00, cut by the consigne “Plan canicule” 18:00–20:00”, with the day's seats, a window outside every slot if there is one, and three links: the stand's form, the day template of the day and the day's consigne.
aide.ouvertures.anciennesVues: The day laid on the time axis became the Planning page, once a planning is computed; before that, an old address of that view opens the grid on that single day. The combined calendar became the rendering of the cells: its address opens the grid with the same layers.

aide.views.def.planning: The planning first: the title on one line, then the day, the filters and the rendering. The day is chosen on a foldable mini-month, each cell marked with its empty seats, its review, its lock and its consigne; “today” there is the server's date, never your computer's. The Stand and Staff filters are typed: two letters are enough. Below, the review bar and the consigne of the day, one line each. “Print this day” opens the whole day laid out for paper, the wall display's layout, with no link to create; “Show on the TV” leads to Settings, Wall display tab, where the television's link and its QR code are created. “By day”, “By stand”, “By person” and “By typologie” choose the axis: the day, or the whole event read stand by stand, person by person or typologie by typologie; the Stand, Staff member, Location and Typologie filters follow from one axis to the next. The month, the meal load, the location graph, the Hours, the Fairness screen, the Rest days, the Heatmap, the Hours breakdown and the Plan by typologie, once screens of their own, are here: their old addresses lead here.

aide.views.def.parStand: The second axis of the Planning page: one line per stand, one column per day, and in each cell the people holding its seats — the sheet usually kept in a spreadsheet, with what a spreadsheet does not compute. The cell is coloured by its coverage: filled, partial, empty in red; a stand closed that day is greyed and hatched, which is not a gap. “Names”, “Counters” (2/2) or “Coverage” (the colour alone) choose what the cell says. On the right, the seats to fill, the filled ones, the share of seat-hours held and the hours to fill; at the foot, for each day, the filled seats over the seats to fill. A click or Enter on a cell opens the seat panel on that stand that day — its first empty seat, otherwise its first seat —, the stand's name leads to its record, and the arrows move through the grid.
aide.views.def.parPersonne: The third axis: one line per staff member, one column per day, and in each cell the day's stand and hours, coloured by what the person does — working, resting, unavailable; a border marks a day that runs into the evening, and a red cell an assignment made on a day declared unavailable. On the right, what each person received: hours and gap to the median, hours per week, evening, weekend, public holidays, Sunday, “Night (payroll)”, seats, demanding seats, distinct stands, typologies and locations, wishes and appreciations honoured, days worked, rest days, longest streak. Every column sorts with a click on its title; the columns where everyone is at zero stay hidden until “Always-empty columns” is ticked. There is only one evening in the application: the time set in the legal parameters, which the legend recalls; the fixed 10 pm bound only serves “Night (payroll)”, for the payroll. “Timeline” draws one proportional bar per person, which fits a month-long event on one screen. “Hours for the payroll (CSV)” and “Fairness (CSV)” export the two usual files. A click on a cell opens the seat panel on the person's first seat that day; their name leads to their profile, whose “Load and fairness” section reads their indicators one under the other next to a radar: one axis per indicator — hours, evenings, week-ends, demanding seats, honoured wishes, and optionally public holidays, appreciations, worked days, longest run. Each axis runs from the edition's minimum, at the centre, to its maximum, at the rim; the filled polygon is the person, the dotted one the median, the grey area the range. Further out means more loaded, except on the axes marked “↑ better”. An axis where everybody has the same value is drawn at the centre and says “no spread”. “Compare with…” lays a second person on the same radar, to arbitrate between two.
aide.views.def.parTypologie: The fourth axis: the saved plan read by game typologie, in one table — seats, hours, cap per staff member, people assigned, vetted, vetted never assigned, assigned without the skill. Every figure leads to the screen where you act on it: the seats and the hours to “By stand” narrowed to the typologie, the vetted to the Staff page filtered on it, the ones assigned without the skill to the Skills grid on its column. A stand offering several typologies counts one seat in each.

aide.calculer.entrees: The page opens on what stands in the way of a schedule without breaches — feasibility and alerts —, then on “This solve will take into account”: the locks, the manual adjustments, the consignes and their dates, the availability declarations still waiting — which the solve will not see —, the rules switched off and the changes made since the last solve. Each counter leads to the screen that lists them; a counter at zero stays shown, muted. Then come the three buttons, each with its sentence. After a solve, its result reads in sentences, and “View the schedule”, “Review” — the first day not reviewed yet — and “Publish” are right below. The volumetry of the problem is folded at the bottom of the page; the solve budget is set in Planning rules, Solve tab.
aide.adHoc.liste: The dialog starts with the person, then the type: one thinks “Alice”, not “incompatibility”. The “Person” field above the list keeps only the adjustments naming someone — by name or id; an animateur's fiche leads there filtered on them. The address keeps the filter.
aide.consignesSolveur.relancer: After any entry on one of the three tabs — an adjustment, a lock, a consigne —, the page offers “Run the solve again” in place: a correction when a plan exists, which only re-opens what the entry invalidated, otherwise a full solve. The Solver counts these entries in “This solve will take into account”.
